## [Unreleased]

### Upgrade notes

- **`itervox --tui` no longer starts a terminal UI** (#240). It prints a pointer to `itervox watch` and exits with code 2, so a unit file or script that still passes `--tui` fails to start: remove the flag. Watch the daemon with `itervox watch` (a live panel) and act with `itervox reply`, `approve`, `pause`, `resume`, `dispatch` and `workers`.

- **The first daemon on a machine now also serves the hub on `127.0.0.1:8089`** (#228). With `hub.enabled` on by default, the first daemon started (and, after it stops, the next one) opens a second, loopback-only listener for the hub; if 8089 is busy it takes the next free port. Every hub route except its health probe needs a hub token (`itervox token create --hub`), so nothing new is reachable without one. Each daemon's registry record gains `hub_member`, and a daemon the hub proxies gets `hub-viewer` / `hub-operator` tokens in its own token store (listed by `itervox token list`). Start a daemon with `--no-hub`, or set `hub.enabled: false` (for example in `~/.itervox/settings.jsonc`), to keep the old behaviour.

- **Existing shared bare clones are migrated on first use** (#195). The first time the daemon creates a worktree after the upgrade, `<workspace.root>/.bare` has its `remote.origin.fetch` rewritten from `+refs/heads/*:refs/heads/*` to `+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*` (any other refspec you added is kept), is fetched once to populate `refs/remotes/origin/*`, and then has every `branch.<name>.merge` that points at a different branch on origin (the #193 layout) repointed at `refs/heads/<name>` when origin has that branch, or unset when it does not. Upstreams on other remotes are left alone. No branch, commit or worktree is deleted or moved: local branches that used to mirror origin stay as they are. The migration is idempotent and needs no action; `itervox doctor` shows whether a clone is still on the old refspec and when it last fetched.

- **Guardrails are on by default** (#204). After the upgrade, agents Itervox starts may push only to their issue branch (no pushes to `main`/`master`/`develop`/the base branch, no tag pushes, no force pushes or branch deletions), never merge their own pull request, and wait for a human approval before `vercel --prod`, `fly deploy`, `kubectl apply`, `terraform apply`, `gcloud deploy`, `npm publish` or `cargo publish`. A workflow whose prompt tells agents to rebase and force-push, or to push a second branch, now gets a refusal explaining what to do instead; set `guardrails.allow_force_push: true` or `guardrails.enabled: false` to keep the old behaviour. Guarded agents no longer see `ITERVOX_API_TOKEN`. `itervox init --update` writes the `guardrails:` block with its defaults.

- **Playbooks are on by default** (#218). `itervox init --update` now writes `.itervox/playbooks/{bug-fix,feature,refactor,perf,investigation,docs}.md` (never overwriting a file you have) and, when the root `.gitignore` ignores `.itervox/`, the `!.itervox/playbooks/` carve-outs. From then on a worker run whose issue has a mapped label (`bug`, `feature`, `refactor`, `perf`, `docs`, …) or a confidently matching title and description gets that playbook in its prompt, which also changes its prompt-version digest. Runs that get no playbook keep their digest. Set `agent.playbooks.enabled: false`, delete the files, or choose **None** on an issue to opt out.

- **Settings files now win over WORKFLOW.md's front matter, and the front matter is deprecated for the runtime sections** (#239). Every existing `WORKFLOW.md` keeps loading and behaving the same, on `itervox_schema_version: 2`: a key its front matter sets still applies. The order is now defaults < `~/.itervox/settings.jsonc` (your personal defaults) < `WORKFLOW.md` front matter < `.itervox/settings.jsonc` < `.itervox/settings.local.jsonc`. The only precedence change is that when the project or local settings file sets the same key as the front matter, that file now wins (it used to lose), and the conflict is reported once (`itervox doctor` `WARNING:` line, one startup-log line per key); the front matter still wins over the user file, which is not reported. New projects from `itervox init` and `itervox quickstart` start with these sections in `.itervox/settings.jsonc`. `itervox doctor` lists each layered front-matter key as `deprecated:` with where it moves, and the startup log names them once. To move them, run `itervox init --update --workflow WORKFLOW.md` (preview with `--dry-run`; `WORKFLOW.md.bak` is written first). Dashboard saves of tracker states, the failed state, the project filter and tracker scope, `dependencies.analysis_mode` and automations now write `.itervox/settings.jsonc` (or `.itervox/settings.local.jsonc` when it already sets the key) and remove the key from `WORKFLOW.md`; a cleared scope key is removed instead of commented out. A hand edit of a settings file reloads the daemon like an edit of `WORKFLOW.md` (#245). Guide: [Moving settings out of WORKFLOW.md](site/src/content/docs/guides/settings-migration.mdx).

### Added

- **The daemon reloads when a settings file changes** (#245). The user (`~/.itervox/settings.jsonc`, or `$ITERVOX_USER_SETTINGS`), project (`.itervox/settings.jsonc`) and local (`.itervox/settings.local.jsonc`) settings files are watched together with `WORKFLOW.md`, with the same 2-second debounce, the same validation and the same drain-then-reload; an edit that touches several of them at once (`itervox init --update`) reloads once. A file that does not exist yet is watched by its path, so creating it (and its `.itervox/` directory) is picked up, and deleting it reloads without that layer. Itervox's own writes (Settings page saves, the Models refresh button) never reload, as for `WORKFLOW.md`; `itervox config set` and `itervox init --update` run as other processes, so a running daemon reloads exactly once for each. An edit that does not load — to any of the four files — no longer drains the daemon: the running generation keeps its config, the log gets one error naming the file (and the line, for a settings file that does not parse or sets a section of the wrong shape), and the dashboard's banner names the file until an edit fixes it. `itervox doctor` lists the watched files (`watched: …`), including the ones that do not exist yet.

- **Project rail and Homebrew cask for the Mac app** (#244). Every dashboard window has a collapsible project rail: pinned projects, then the hub's members, the daemons outside the hub (and stopped projects you added), and remote daemons grouped by host, each with its name, a health dot (running, stopped, unreachable, token required), the running-agent count and a badge for questions and guardrail approvals waiting for you. It shows what the menu-bar refresh already read (the hub's one projects request, per-daemon reads otherwise, the tunnels for remotes) and adds no polling. Clicking a row shows that project's dashboard in the same window, with the token handed over by the same initialization script as before and never in a URL; ⌘1…⌘9 jump to the first nine projects, ⌘⇧] / ⌘⇧[ step between them and ⌥⌘S collapses the rail (the new **Projects** menu). Rows can be pinned and dragged into order (or moved with ⌥↑/⌥↓); the order, the pins and the collapsed state are saved in `projects.json`. **Open in New Window** is on each row's context menu, and the menu bar's **Open Dashboard** and notifications still open a project in the window showing it or a new one. The rail is keyboard and screen-reader accessible (arrow keys, roving focus, labelled dots and badges). It is an app-local page in its own webview beside the dashboard: it has no IPC, no network access and never sees a token, and the dashboard webview gets no new permissions. The desktop release workflow now renders `Casks/itervox-app.rb` (version, the DMG's SHA-256, `depends_on macos: ">= :big_sur"`, `auto_updates true`; `desktop/scripts/homebrew-cask.sh`) and commits it to `vnovick/homebrew-tap` with the formula's `HOMEBREW_TAP_GITHUB_TOKEN`, only after notarization succeeded and the DMG is on the release, and never for an unsigned build or a pre-release: `brew install --cask vnovick/tap/itervox-app`. The [Mac app guide](site/src/content/docs/guides/mac-app.mdx#install) covers the three install paths (DMG, Homebrew, `make desktop` from source, none needing an Apple ID), the rail and its shortcuts; CONTRIBUTING lists the release secrets.

- **`itervox watch` is a live terminal panel** (#240). A status header (running against slots, queued, retrying, waiting for you, waiting for a slot, blocked by dependencies with a `slot-bound` / `dependency-bound` line, paused, `ALL DISPATCH PAUSED`, and the hub when this daemon serves it); one lane per running issue with its title, profile and backend, elapsed time and turn, tokens and estimated cost, and its latest activity (the run context's last tool call and step, redacted, control characters dropped); the feed's events as they happen, read by cursor so a dropped connection or a restart continues where it left off and a gap is reported; and every input request and guardrail approval highlighted with the exact `itervox reply …` / `itervox approve …` command (with the `--workflow`, `--url` or `--project` that reaches the same daemon) — it never answers by itself. Coloured by state on a terminal (`NO_COLOR` and `TERM=dumb` respected), plain text in a pipe. New flags: `--issue ID` (the issue's full redacted log and its events), `--project NAME` (one project through the machine's hub, with `ITERVOX_HUB_TOKEN`; the other client commands take it too), `--events-only`, `--json` (one JSON object per line: `status`, `event`, `gap`, `log`) and `--since SEQ` (replay after a feed cursor; watch prints the cursor when it stops). It never reads stdin and never changes the terminal mode, so it works over SSH, in tmux and without a terminal. New `itervox approve <issue>` answers a guardrail approval (and refuses for an ordinary question). The `/api/v1/state` rows gain `running[].title`, `running[].profile`, `running[].costUsdEstimated` and `inputRequired[].guardrailApproval`, and `running[].lastEvent` is now redacted. See the [terminal guide](https://itervox.dev/guides/terminal/).

- **Change review: line comments, PR reviews and open in editor** (#238). In an issue's Changes tab, click a line number (shift-click for a range) to comment: **Send to the agent** queues a steering message for the live run that names the file and lines and quotes the selected diff lines; **Post on the PR** posts a GitHub review comment, now or as a pending comment. **Comment**, **Request changes** and **Approve** submit one GitHub review with every pending comment; Itervox never merges from it, the `merge_pr` gate and `agent.review_quorum` are unchanged, and the response lists the PR's merge-block labels and the agent quorum. Once an issue has a GitHub PR, `GET /api/v1/issues/{identifier}/diff` serves the PR's files (`base...head`) by default, with `?source=worktree` for the live worktree while a run is live; the response gains `source`, `sources`, `prUrl`, `headSha`, `prError` and `worktreePath`. New operator routes `POST /api/v1/issues/{identifier}/review-comments` and `POST /api/v1/issues/{identifier}/pr-review` use the PR-event watcher's GitHub credentials. Each file links to VS Code or Cursor (chosen under Settings → Editor) when the dashboard runs on the daemon's machine, and shows a copyable path otherwise. Feed events `review_comment_posted` and `pr_review_submitted_by_operator` carry no comment text; the snapshot advertises the `change_review` capability.

- **The Mac app uses the hub** (#232). When a local hub runs (`~/.itervox/daemons/hub.lock`), the app reads every hub member from one `GET /hub/api/v1/projects` per refresh (each member's summary) over its single #229 events stream, instead of polling each member daemon; the stream's `projects` events wake the refresh at once, and hub members no longer hold the app in its 3-second busy interval. Daemons that are not members (`--no-hub`, older releases, members the hub cannot read) keep the #212 per-daemon polling, and when the hub stops (the stream ends or the projects read fails) every daemon is polled again until a new hub takes over; after a takeover the stream reads the new hub's notifications from the start of its ring. The tray shows the hub's status and member count (`Hub · 3 projects`, `Hub: connecting…`, `Hub unreachable — polling each project`, `Hub: not running — each project polled`) with **Open Hub Dashboard**, **Phone…** (the hub page's Phones view with the #231 pairing QR code) and **Notification Settings…** (the #229 settings view), opened in the hub window with an admin hub token the app creates on first use (`itervox-desktop-admin`, Keychain entry `itervox-hub-admin`; the events stream keeps its viewer token). The hub page opens on the view named in `?view=` (`projects`, `notifications`, `phones`). Remote daemons over SSH or IAP stay as they are, but a host whose daemons form a hub is reached through one tunnel to that hub: Add Remote and Refresh Daemon List also run `itervox hub --json` on the host, create an operator hub token there (`itervox-desktop`), and read and open every member through the hub's proxy (`/hub/p/{project}/`), health-checking the hub tunnel on `/hub/api/v1/health`; non-members keep their own tunnels, and if the hub tunnel stops answering each member gets its own tunnel again until it does. Guides: [Mac app](site/src/content/docs/guides/mac-app.mdx#with-a-hub-v029), [The itervox hub](site/src/content/docs/guides/hub.mdx#the-mac-app).

- **Your phone: the hub as an installable web app, QR pairing and Web Push** (#231). The hub serves the dashboard as a web app you can install (`/manifest.webmanifest`, icons and a push-only service worker `/sw.js` in the embedded bundle, linked and registered only on the hub's pages, never on a daemon's own dashboard) with a phone layout: `/hub/m` lists what needs you across every project (questions and guardrail approvals, failed runs) and the projects, and `/hub/p/{project}/m/{issue}` shows the run now, a reply box or **Approve** / **Reject**, the steering chips and **Pause dispatch** / **Resume dispatch** — the dashboard's own components over the project's proxied API, in separate lazy chunks (the bundle budget passes unchanged). **Pairing:** the hub page's new **Phones** view (admin) shows a QR code for `/hub/pair#code=…` with a 160-bit one-time code that expires after 10 minutes (`POST /hub/api/v1/pairing`, admin); the phone names itself and trades the code (`POST /hub/api/v1/pairing/exchange`, no token, throttled after 10 wrong codes a minute) for its own operator hub token `device: <name>`, kept on the device; `GET`/`DELETE /hub/api/v1/devices[/{id}]` (admin) list and revoke paired devices, which stops the token and its pushes at once. **Web Push:** a built-in `push` channel of the #229 notification settings (routing, snooze and digests unchanged) sends to every device subscribed with `POST /hub/api/v1/push/subscribe` (operator; a name and `PushSubscription.toJSON()`, https endpoints on Google, Mozilla, Apple and Microsoft push services only, stored `0600` in `~/.itervox/hub/push_subscriptions.json`, listed with `GET /hub/api/v1/push/devices` and removed with `DELETE /hub/api/v1/push/devices/{id}`). A push carries only `{kind, project, issue, title, url}` — a redacted title of at most 80 characters and a deep link, never agent output — encrypted per RFC 8291 (aes128gcm) with the standard library only (`crypto/ecdh`, `crypto/hkdf`, AES-GCM; checked against the RFC's Appendix A vector) and signed with a VAPID key generated on first use in `~/.itervox/hub/push_vapid.pem` (`0600`; `GET /hub/api/v1/push/vapid-public-key`, viewer). A device the push service drops (404/410) or whose token is revoked is removed. **`server.allowed_origins`** (new, load-time, default empty = same-origin only) is a CORS allow-list for the daemon's API and, on the daemon serving it, the hub: a listed origin gets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for itself and its preflights answered; every other cross-origin preflight now gets 403 `origin_not_allowed`. The dashboard's API origin is configurable at build time (`VITE_API_ORIGIN`) and at runtime (`<meta name="itervox-api-origin">` in the served `index.html`), so the same bundle runs embedded or hosted elsewhere. No new Go module; one small web dependency, `uqr` (MIT), draws the QR code in the hub chunk. Guide: [Your phone](site/src/content/docs/guides/phone.mdx) (LAN, Tailscale, your own tunnel); configuration: [`server.allowed_origins`](site/src/content/docs/configuration.mdx#server); API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#hub).

- **Hub Slack: your own Slack app over Socket Mode — alerts, replies, approvals and steering** (#230). The hub can post to Slack through an app you create yourself in your workspace and take your answers back. `itervox hub slack setup` prints the app manifest (Socket Mode on, interactivity on, the `/itervox` command, bot scopes `chat:write`, `commands` and `im:write`; `--json`, `--manifest-only`) and the steps, stores the app-level (`xapp-…`) and bot (`xoxb-…`) tokens with echo off in the hub's own `~/.itervox/hub/.env` (`0600`; also `itervox secret set KEY --hub`), never printing or logging them, and writes the allowed users and a channel (or DM) per hub project to `~/.itervox/settings.jsonc`; `itervox hub slack status [--json]` shows what is set. New load-time settings `hub.slack.enabled` (default `false`), `hub.slack.allowed_users` (Slack user IDs that may act; **empty means nobody**, messages are alerts only), `hub.slack.channels` and `hub.slack.default_channel`, IDs checked at load. The daemon serving the hub holds the workspace's single Socket Mode connection (it moves with the hub), acknowledges every envelope, reconnects at once on a `disconnect` and with backoff (1 s to 2 min) otherwise; it is an HTTP client only, no inbound port. Slack is the `slack` channel of the #229 notification settings (routing, snooze and digests unchanged; a digest is one message): an input request arrives with the question and a reply box, a guardrail approval with **Approve** and **Reject**, a failed run or review verdict with a dashboard link, and `/itervox steer [project/]ISSUE text` steers a live run through `POST /api/v1/sessions/{runId}/message`. Each button and reply box carries a value the hub signs (HMAC-SHA256 with `~/.itervox/hub/slack_actions.key`) binding project, member daemon, issue, run and kind, valid 7 days; the hub then checks the Slack user is allowed, the member is still the one signed for, the request is still pending and the value was not used (a second click gets an ephemeral "already handled"), and calls the member through the new `hub.MemberActions` (the member's own route table, viewer/operator routes only, the hub's member token). Answers are human replies: `POST /api/v1/issues/{identifier}/provide-input` gains an optional `via: "slack"` (a closed enum, refused with `fromAgent`), recorded on the `input_answered`, `guardrail_approved` and `guardrail_blocked` feed events and mirrored to the tracker like a dashboard answer. Every Slack action is logged with the Slack user ID, project, issue, action and outcome, never the text. The WebSocket uses `golang.org/x/net/websocket` from the existing `golang.org/x/net` dependency (no new module). Hub notifications gain an optional `runId`. Guide: [Slack](site/src/content/docs/guides/slack.mdx); configuration: [`hub`](site/src/content/docs/configuration.mdx#hub); API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md).

- **Hub notifications: per-project routing, digests, snooze and desktop notifications** (#229). The hub turns its merged feed into notifications you control, from `~/.itervox/hub/notifications.json` (`0600`, written atomically; published schema [`notifications.schema.json`](site/public/schema/notifications.schema.json), kept in step with the parser by a test). Per project and per kind — input required, guardrail approval (an `input_required` feed event whose payload kind is `guardrail_approval`), run failed, review verdict, PR merged, lesson proposed, dispatch paused — it routes to the channels `push`, `slack` and `desktop`; input required, guardrail approval and run failed go to every enabled channel by default and the rest are off. There is no budget kind: a #136 budget pause emits no feed event yet. A project can be snoozed until a time (its notifications are dropped until then). Urgent kinds (input, approval) are sent at once; the others are batched into one digest per channel at most every `digest_interval_minutes` (default 15). Routing, snooze and digests are hub state, never a member's or the orchestrator's. Channels plug in through `hub.Channel` (delivery only) and `hub.Config.Channels`; every channel shares one routing decision, `NotificationSettings.Route`, which Slack (#230) and Web Push (#231) will call. The built-in desktop channel sends `event: notification` frames on `GET /hub/api/v1/events` (resumable with `notify_since` / `Last-Event-ID`), and `GET /hub/api/v1/feed` events now carry `notifyKind` and `channels`. New routes, declared in the hub's route table: `GET`/`PUT /hub/api/v1/notifications` (admin) and `POST /hub/api/v1/notifications/test` (operator). The hub dashboard gains **Notifications** (admin): a project × kind × channel matrix, a snooze per project, the digest interval and a **Send test** button per channel. The Mac app, when a local hub runs, holds one events stream with a viewer hub token it creates for itself (`itervox-desktop`, in the Keychain) and shows the hub's desktop notifications natively instead of its per-daemon alerts for local projects, falling back to them when the hub stops. Guide: [Notifications](site/src/content/docs/guides/hub.mdx#notifications); API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#get--put-hubapiv1notifications).

- **The itervox hub: one URL, a scoped proxy and a merged feed for every project on a machine** (#228). The first daemon started on a machine becomes the hub: it takes a `flock`'d `~/.itervox/daemons/hub.lock` (which then holds its address, never a token), and when it stops — cleanly or killed — the next live daemon takes over within about a second (fsnotify on the lock plus a one-second retry; tested with a `SIGKILL`ed process). Members are the live registry records with the new `hub_member: true`, refreshed on every registry change and every 10 s. On `hub.bind:hub.port` (default `127.0.0.1:8089`, the next free port when busy) the hub serves `GET /hub/api/v1/projects` (each member's summary, health, version and capabilities), `/hub/p/{project}/api/v1/...` (a reverse proxy to that member: the hub token's scope is checked first against the member's own route table from the new viewer route `GET /api/v1/route-scopes`, the caller's `Authorization` is dropped and the hub's `hub-viewer` or `hub-operator` token in the member's store injected — created and remembered `0600` through the `itervox mcp` code path, never printed; member admin routes, agent grants and webhooks are never proxied; SSE passes through; a member 401 becomes 502), `GET /hub/api/v1/feed?since=` (every member's #213 feed merged in one growing hub sequence, each event with its `project`, resumable from per-member cursors in `~/.itervox/hub/hub_feed_cursors.json`), `GET /hub/api/v1/events` (SSE announcements), and the dashboard at `/hub/` with a project switcher. The hub has its own token store (`~/.itervox/hub/tokens.json`, `itervox token ... --hub`) and no unauthenticated mode. Merged events go to every enabled `Notifier` (`Name`, `Enabled(project, kind)`, `Notify(ctx, Event)`) at least once, with a per-notifier cursor and backoff; v0.2.9 ships the `log` notifier. The dashboard reads its API base path from one place (`web/src/auth/apiBase.ts`, default `/api/v1`, `VITE_API_BASE` at build time), so the unchanged per-project dashboard runs under `/hub/p/{project}/`. `GET /api/v1/summary` gains `capabilities`. New: `itervox hub [--json]`, `itervox --no-hub`, `hub.enabled` / `hub.port` / `hub.bind` (load-time; a new `hub` section in the settings layers). The hub runs in a daemon process but outside its orchestrator event loop and reaches its own project only over HTTP. Guide: [The itervox hub](site/src/content/docs/guides/hub.mdx); configuration: [`hub`](site/src/content/docs/configuration.mdx#hub); API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#hub).

- **Playbooks per task type, a decision log and steering phrases** (#218). **Playbooks:** Markdown files in `.itervox/playbooks/<name>.md` (committable; `itervox init` scaffolds `bug-fix`, `feature`, `refactor`, `perf`, `investigation` and `docs`, and `init --update` adds the missing ones) tell a worker run how to approach its kind of work. Each dispatch reads the directory again and picks one: the operator's per-issue choice (the issue detail's **Playbook** picker, `POST /api/v1/issues/{identifier}/playbook`, operator; event-loop state persisted to `.itervox/playbook_overrides.json`), else the first issue label mapped by `agent.playbooks.labels` (documented defaults such as `bug` → `bug-fix`), else a keyword classifier over the title and description (title hits score 2, description hits 1; attached only at 2 or more and strictly ahead of every other playbook), else none. The issue card shows the playbook. It is inserted as a `## Playbook: <name>` block right after `INSTRUCTIONS.md` and is a prompt-digest component only when present, so existing digests do not change; the eval composer renders and digests it the same way. Reviewer and automation runs get none. A playbook's frontmatter `require_evidence` joins the profile's in the existing #80 evidence gate. **Decision log:** the Run Context names `run.decisions_path` (`{{ run.decisions_path }}`), `<timestamp>_<profile>.decisions.tsv` next to the run's handoff, where agents append `time⇥decision⇥why⇥alternative` lines; `GET /api/v1/issues/{identifier}/decisions` (viewer) parses every run's log defensively (64 KiB, 200 rows, 50 runs, 500-byte fields, redacted) and the issue detail shows them as a timeline. **Steering phrases:** the Sessions composer and a new **Steer the run** box in the issue detail have one-click chips ("Prove it works", "Fix the root cause", "Smallest change", "Reproduce first", "Explain the number", "Subtract before you add") that send a documented message through the existing steering endpoint; the list is `sessions.steering_phrases` (`GET /api/v1/steering/phrases`). **Verification readiness:** Repo Analysis readiness and `itervox doctor` gain a `verify_skill` check that warns when the repository has no `.claude/skills/*verif*/SKILL.md`, `scripts/verify*`, `make verify` target or `package.json` `verify` script; **Generate verify skill** (`POST /api/v1/repo/readiness/verify-skill-issue`, operator) creates a tracker issue asking an agent to write one, the same way an accepted enforcement suggestion does. Guide: [Playbooks, decisions & steering](site/src/content/docs/guides/playbooks.mdx); configuration: [`agent.playbooks`](site/src/content/docs/configuration.mdx#playbooks), [`sessions.steering_phrases`](site/src/content/docs/configuration.mdx#sessions); API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#playbooks-decisions-and-steering-218).

- **Lessons round 2: reviewer and revert triggers, recipe lessons, lesson to rule, enforcement suggestions** (#217). Three more lesson triggers: a change reviewers' blocking verdicts asked for at least twice across runs or issues (`reviewer_ask`, matched by the same normalized-word similarity as lesson dedupe; the daemon's own verdict notes never count); a merged agent PR reverted on the base branch (`reverted_pr`, found every 30 minutes off the event loop by #201's revert detection, read-only through gitexec, and proposed on the issue of the run that opened the PR); and a hard-won success (`recipe`: a worker run that succeeded after at least `memory.lessons.recipe_min_failed_runs` failed attempts, default 2, a steering message, or `recipe_min_turns` turns, default 40), whose lesson is what worked and the verification that proved it, read from the run's handoff ("Recipe: when …, … Verify with: …"). In the Lessons tab's new **Approved** view, each approved lesson shows its analytics (times applied, the runs in history that used it and how they ended) and can be **promoted to a rule** in the user or project rules layer (`POST /api/v1/memory/{id}/promote-to-rule`, admin like the Rules editor): the rule `lesson-<id>` links back to the lesson, which is archived with a pointer to the rule. Once a lesson has been seen `memory.lessons.enforce_threshold` times (default 3), the same budgeted drafting call (template fallback) suggests the strongest enforcement it can, preferring a lint rule, a type, a test, a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md rule, then an Itervox rule; **Create Enforce issue** (`POST /api/v1/memory/{id}/enforcement/accept`, operator) creates an "Enforce: …" tracker issue carrying the draft and the evidence, in `memory.lessons.enforce_issue_state` (default: the first backlog state), so an agent implements it like any other issue; Itervox never commits code itself. **Dismiss** turns a suggestion down for good. "Not helping" gains an **enforced** state. A lesson sighting whose runs are all already in its evidence no longer raises its count. New lesson fields `verification`, `rule` and `enforcement` are in the published memory schema.

- **`itervox mcp`: a local MCP server for the board and memory** (#216). New `itervox mcp` serves the Model Context Protocol over stdio (one JSON message per line; stdout carries protocol only, diagnostics go to stderr) so Claude Code (`claude mcp add itervox -- itervox mcp`), Claude Desktop and Codex can reach the running daemon of the project. It finds the daemon like `itervox status --json` (host registry, then process scan, then `.itervox/dashboard_url`; `--project` or `--url` to choose) and is a plain HTTP client of its API, so the daemon's scope checks, redaction and approval rules apply unchanged. On first use it creates a stored `viewer` token named `mcp` through the token store and remembers the secret in `.itervox/mcp-token.json` (0600, gitignored; never printed or logged); `--token-scope operator` creates an operator token instead, and `--token` / `ITERVOX_TOKEN` use a given one. Read tools: `board_summary`, `list_issues`, `get_issue` (with the #215 run context), `explain_blockers` (dependency audit and inferred dependencies), `recent_failures`, `feed_since` (the #213 cursor feed) and `recall` (memory ranked exactly like run-time retrieval, within a token budget). Write tools, listed only for an operator token: `dispatch` (refused while all dispatch is paused), `pause_dispatch`, `resume_dispatch`, `reply_input` (never answers a guardrail approval), `steer` and `remember` (creates a `proposed` entry for the lessons review queue, never an active one). Results are compact JSON, secrets are redacted and agent output is never returned. The protocol is a small built-in JSON-RPC 2.0 implementation (initialize with version negotiation, ping, tools/list, tools/call) rather than the official Go SDK, whose v1 module brings JWT, OAuth, assembly-backed JSON and `x/tools` dependencies for transports this stdio server does not use. API: new `GET /api/v1/memory/recall?q=&profile=&budget=` (viewer) and an optional `fromAgent` flag on `POST /api/v1/issues/{identifier}/provide-input` that takes the agent path, so a relayed reply can never answer a guardrail approval. Guide: [MCP server](site/src/content/docs/guides/mcp.mdx); CLI: [`itervox mcp`](site/src/content/docs/cli.mdx); API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#memory).

- **Run context and worktree diff endpoints, with Now and Changes views** (#215). New `GET /api/v1/issues/{identifier}/context`: the issue's current run (or its latest finished one, the 32 newest kept for the session) — run ID, profile, backend, start time, the current step (the last assistant message, redacted, whitespace-collapsed, cut to 500 bytes), the last tool call (name and target — file, command, pattern — redacted and cut to 300 bytes; computed from the call's input with every output field removed, so tool output never appears), tool-call and turn counts, tokens, a pending input or guardrail approval, delivered and queued steering messages, guardrail blocks in this run, plus the worktree's changed files and its handoffs (titles and paths). Workers build it from the stream the claude and codex parsers already emit (`agent.TurnResult` gains `LastToolName`, `LastToolTarget`, `ToolCalls`) and send it to the event loop at most once a second per run plus once per turn (`EventRunContext`, non-blocking); the loop keeps it in `State.RunContexts` keyed by run ID and publishes it without an SSE frame, so the snapshot and `/events` are unchanged. New `GET /api/v1/issues/{identifier}/diff[?base=][&file=]`: the worktree (commits, uncommitted edits, untracked files) against the merge base of `HEAD` with the run's pull-request base (the blocker branch when stacked, else `workspace.base_branch`), with each file's status and line counts; `?file=` returns that file's unified diff, cut at 256 KiB on a line boundary, binary files detected. All git calls go through `internal/gitexec` on the request goroutine (never the event loop) under a 15 s timeout; it works for finished issues whose worktree still exists and answers `404 no_worktree` otherwise; `?base=` accepts branch names only and `?file=` only a path in the diff. Both routes are viewer reads; a file's hunks need operator (an agent can commit a secret) and are redacted below admin. Dashboard: the issue detail gains a **Now** panel (current step, last tool call, waits, changed files, handoffs; polls while the run is live) and a **Changes** tab with the file list and a lazy-loaded unified diff viewer rendered as text; a viewer sees the list only. Advertised as the `run_context` capability. Guide: [Now & Changes](site/src/content/docs/guides/now-and-changes.mdx); API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#run-context-and-changes-215).

- **Token scopes (viewer, operator, admin) and rotation without restart** (#214). Named API tokens in `.itervox/tokens.json` (gitignored, mode 0600, SHA-256 hashes only; secrets start with `itx_` and are printed once) with a scope: `viewer` reads state, logs and the SSE streams with secrets redacted (inline env-assignment values in profile commands, URL credentials, known key shapes, and the raw text of settings files); `operator` adds dispatch and issue control, steering, input replies, approvals, dispatch pause/resume, memory edits and log clearing; `admin` adds settings, token management, tmux control, workspace deletion and the automations configuration. The existing `ITERVOX_API_TOKEN`, the auto-generated token and the Mac app's supervisor token stay admin, so nothing changes for current setups; `server.allow_unauthenticated` keeps every caller admin (its startup warning now says stored tokens are not consulted). Every route declares its scope in one table (`internal/server/route_scopes.go`) that the middleware enforces; an undeclared route is refused, a test walks the router so a new route without a declaration fails CI, and a refusal answers `403 insufficient_scope` naming the needed scope (body and `X-Itervox-Required-Scope`). New `itervox token create --name --scope [--expires]`, `list`, `revoke <id>` and `rotate [<id>]` (no id: the one stored admin token) write the file directly whether or not the daemon runs; a running daemon picks up a CLI change within a second (mtime/inode check, cross-process `flock`) and an API change at once — no restart. Each create, revoke and rotate is logged without the secret; `lastUsed` is recorded at minute resolution. API: `GET /api/v1/whoami`, `GET|POST /api/v1/tokens`, `DELETE /api/v1/tokens/{id}`, `POST /api/v1/tokens/{id}/rotate` (admin), and `callerScope` on `GET /state` and every `/events` frame. Dashboard: **Settings → Access** lists, creates, rotates and revokes tokens (admin only); the Settings page, dispatch pause toggle and input-reply boxes hide what the caller's scope cannot use, and a `403 insufficient_scope` raises a toast. Agent-action and guardrail grants are unchanged. Guide: [Security & access tokens](site/src/content/docs/guides/security.mdx); API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#token-scopes-214).

- **Guardrails: pushes only to the issue branch, no self-merge, approval for deploy commands** (#204). New `internal/guardrails` and a `guardrails:` config block (`enabled`, default true; `allow_force_push`, default false; `approval_commands`, glob-token patterns, default the seven deploy/publish commands above; read at startup). Each local dispatched run, and each tmux session started with **New session**, gets a private runtime directory: PATH shims for `gh`, `glab`, `git` and the approval-command programs, put first on the agent's PATH, and git hooks through `core.hooksPath` in `GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS`. The pre-push hook refuses pushes to any ref but the issue branch (or, once per run, a new branch the agent created and has checked out), tag pushes, and force pushes and deletions unless `allow_force_push`; every hook then chains to the repository's own hooks directory, so its hooks still run. The shims refuse `gh pr merge`, `glab mr merge`, merge API calls, `git merge` into the default branch, `git push --no-verify` and `-c core.hooksPath=…`, and forward everything else to the real program (resolved past the shims) with the same arguments, input, environment and exit status. A command matching `approval_commands` blocks and raises an input request on the running issue ("Agent wants to run: …") through the existing input-required flow — dashboard, Sessions panel, Mac app and tracker reply; `approve` runs it exactly once, any other reply (or dismissing) rejects it and is passed to the agent as the reason; agents cannot answer it (the agent-actions `provide-input` route is ignored for it); the request is dropped when the run ends and is never persisted. Tmux sessions have no approval channel, so matching commands are refused there. Shims and hooks reach the daemon only through new token-gated routes (`POST /api/v1/agent-actions/{id}/guardrail/events`, `POST …/guardrail/approvals`, `GET …/guardrail/approvals/{id}`, per-run grant with action `guardrail`), which record and decide but never execute anything; commands are redacted before they leave the shim. Every refused or approved operation is logged (`guardrails: …`), written to the issue's log, refusals are recorded in Recent failures (kind `guardrail`) and counted in `itervox_guardrail_blocks_total{kind}`. Known limit, documented: guidance, not a sandbox — an agent that runs git by an absolute path or rewrites its PATH or environment bypasses it, and runs on SSH worker hosts are not guarded in this version (a warning is logged). Guide: [Guardrails](site/src/content/docs/guides/guardrails.mdx); config: [`guardrails`](site/src/content/docs/configuration.mdx#guardrails); API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#guardrail-endpoints-204).

- **Lessons: proposed from corrections and failed-then-succeeded runs, with a review queue** (#203). Itervox now proposes `lesson` memory entries itself, as `status: proposed` (never used by a run until approved), when a human corrects an agent in an input-required reply (dashboard or tracker comment) or a steering message, and when a run that failed or stalled is followed by a successful run on the same issue after a change (the lesson records the steering messages, input replies and blocking reviewer feedback since the failure; a retry that simply worked proposes nothing). Detection runs on the orchestrator's event loop (`State.LessonCorrections`, `State.LessonProposals`); the wording is drafted off the loop by one short call to the lesson profile's backend (`memory.lessons.profile`, by default the reviewer profile) through the agent runner, with no tools, an empty temporary directory, the sandbox permission mode and a hard budget (`draft_token_budget`, default 6000 tokens; `draft_timeout_ms`, default 60 s), falling back to a template ("When …, … Instead of: …") with no profile or a failed call; the result comes back as `EventLessonDrafted`, and the goroutine is joined at shutdown. A near-duplicate (normalized-word similarity of the text or of the correction) bumps the existing lesson's evidence, run ids and confidence instead of proposing another; each issue proposes at most `max_per_issue` (3) per `rate_window_hours` (24). Entries gain an optional `lesson` record (trigger, situation, what went wrong, what worked, the correction, confidence, times seen, drafter, approval time) in the memory file and its schema. The Memory page's **Lessons** tab lists proposals with that evidence and approves them into private or project-shared memory, edits then approves, or rejects them — rejections are remembered in `.itervox/lessons-rejected.json` (normalized words and a fingerprint only, gitignored) so the same lesson is not proposed again; a **Not helping** filter lists approved lessons the last `stale_after_runs` (20) runs did not use or whose runs mostly failed; the sidebar's Memory item shows the queue's count (`proposedLessons` in the snapshot). New `memory.lessons` config (`enabled`, `profile`, `scope`, `auto_approve` per scope, default off, and the limits above; read at startup). API: `POST /api/v1/memory/{id}/approve` (`{scope?, text?}`) and `POST /api/v1/memory/{id}/reject`; `GET /api/v1/memory` gains `lessons` and per-entry `notHelping`. Guide: [Memory → Lessons](site/src/content/docs/guides/memory.mdx#lessons); config: [`memory.lessons`](site/src/content/docs/configuration.mdx#memorylessons); API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#memory).

- **Managed memory: private and project-shared entries, budgeted retrieval and a Memory page** (#202). Itervox now remembers what you tell it between runs. An entry (`preference`, `fact`, `decision` or `lesson`) lives in `~/.itervox/memory.json` (private, never committed; on a remote daemon the daemon user's home, `ITERVOX_USER_MEMORY` to move or `off` to disable it) or `.itervox/memory.json` (project shared, committed). Both are JSON with a published schema (`https://itervox.dev/schema/memory.schema.json`); every save redacts secrets with the daemon's log redaction and rejects entries over 2000 bytes. At each dispatch the daemon reads both files again, always includes pinned entries, ranks the other `active` entries against the issue's title, description and labels and the profile (lexical, no embeddings) and adds them within `memory.token_budget` (default 2000 tokens); rules plus memory stay within `memory.prompt_share_tokens` (default 8000), so the lowest-ranked memories are dropped first and rules never are. The prompt's profile tail is now rules → memory → SOUL.md → INSTRUCTIONS.md (`## Memory` block). Each run records the ids it was given (`memoryIds` in run history), the memory is a prompt-version component (`promptParts.memory`; runs without memory keep their digest), and once the block reaches the agent the entries' `lastUsed` / `useCount` are updated through the orchestrator's event loop. New `memory:` config block (`enabled`, `token_budget`, `prompt_share_tokens`; read at startup). API: `GET`/`POST /api/v1/memory`, `PUT`/`DELETE /api/v1/memory/{id}`, `POST /api/v1/memory/{id}/pin`, `POST /api/v1/memory/{id}/promote` (moves a private entry into the project file and returns its git diff). The new **Memory** page (`/memory`, after Repo Analysis in the sidebar, `g m`, and a **Memory** item in the Mac app's per-daemon menu) searches and filters by type, scope, profile, tag and usage, shows provenance and the runs that used an entry, and edits, pins, archives, deletes (with Undo) and shares entries; "Open in editor" shows the file path with a copy button. Proposed entries wait in a **Lessons** tab and are never used until approved. `itervox init`, `init --update` and daemon startup add the `.itervox/memory.json` carve-outs, and repo readiness checks them.

- **Eval results and failure hotspots in Repo Analysis** (#201). Two new sections on the Repo Analysis page. **Evals** (`/repo#evals`) shows the latest result per profile and scenario: pass or fail, every assertion that failed (missing or forbidden actions, `forbidden_phrases` present, missing marker phrases), the prompt digest it ran against, when, and a **regression** marker when a case passed on the previous digest and fails on the current one. Judged reports are now saved: `make evals` (new; replays the committed recordings through the new `itervox-evals recorded`), `make evals-live`, `make evals-record` and `cmd/itervox-evals` write each report as JSON to `.itervox/evals/<ISO8601>.json` (the directory carries its own `.gitignore`, `itervox init` adds `evals/` to `.itervox/.gitignore`, the newest 20 are kept; `-results-dir`/`EVALS_RESULTS_DIR`), and `GET /api/v1/repo/evals` reads the newest of them; the dashboard never starts an eval run. The digest is the #186 run-history digest: `orchestrator.ComposeEvalPrompt` now returns it (it shares the components with dispatch, so an eval and a dispatched run of the same prompt version agree), live recordings carry it in their `meta` line, and recorded mode reports it only for recordings a live run made; the hand-written fixtures have none. The judges now list every failed assertion, not only the first. **Hotspots** (`/repo#hotspots`) ranks files and directories by failed or stalled runs, reviewer change requests, input requests and reverted agent PRs over the run history, attributed to the files each run's branch changed, with per-signal counts, the issues involved (linked to their logs) and the runs. Run history entries now record the run's branch, PR URL and a reviewer's verdict, written by the event loop. `GET /api/v1/repo/hotspots` returns the latest result of a bounded background job off the event loop: read-only git through `internal/gitexec` (no fetch), one refresh at a time and at most every 10 minutes, at most 100 run lookups per refresh with per-call and per-refresh timeouts, and each run's changed files cached by run ID. The changed files are the branch's diff against its merge base while the branch exists, else the files of the commit on the base that names the PR; reverts are read from the newest 500 base commits; reviews recorded before this release have no verdict — the guide and API reference list these approximations. Guide: [Repo Analysis](site/src/content/docs/guides/repo-analysis.mdx#evals); API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#repo-evals); [docs/evals.md](docs/evals.md#saved-reports-and-the-dashboard).

- **Repo Analysis page; the Skills Inventory moves out of Settings** (#200). A new top-level dashboard page, **Repo Analysis** (`/repo`, in the sidebar after Rules, `g p` in the command palette), gathers repository-level signals in four sections — sub-tabs on wide screens, stacked on phones, each with a deep link: **Capabilities** (`/repo#capabilities`) is the Skills Inventory moved from Settings with no behaviour change (skills, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, hooks, instruction docs, analyzer recommendations with **Fix**, Re-scan; the 785-line card is split into section components); **Runtime usage and cost** (`#usage`) holds the runtime analytics and their recommendations (`HIGH_COST_LOW_USAGE`, `HOOK_STORM`, `CONFIGURED_NOT_LOADED`, `LOADED_NOT_CONFIGURED`) and a new per-profile token breakdown; **Prompt versions** (`#prompts`) lists, per profile, each prompt digest (#186) with first and last seen, runs, success rate and average duration, newest first, and selecting one lists its runs from `GET /api/v1/history?prompt=`; **Agent readiness** (`#readiness`) shows the repository-level `itervox doctor` checks — schema 2 marker, the root `.gitignore` carve-outs for `.itervox/agents/**` and `.itervox/handoff/**`, CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md for the backends in use, the shared bare clone's fetch refspec (#195), skill and subagent references (#86) and tracker reachability — each pass, warn or fail with the fix doctor prints. Settings shows a one-line link instead of the inventory. New `GET /api/v1/repo/readiness`: cmd/itervox injects the provider, and the endpoint and `itervox doctor` build their rows from the same check functions (doctor prints them in a new `repo readiness:` section that does not change its exit code); the checks run on the request goroutine, never on the event loop, and the tracker probe runs under an 8 s timeout even if it ignores its context. `GET /api/v1/history/prompt-versions` rows gain `avgDurationMs`. The Mac app's per-daemon menu (local and remote) has a **Repo Analysis** item that opens `/repo` in the daemon's dashboard window. Guide: [Repo Analysis](site/src/content/docs/guides/repo-analysis.mdx); API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#repo-readiness); [docs/skills-inventory.md](docs/skills-inventory.md) and the site's Skills Inventory guide now point to Repo Analysis → Capabilities.

- **Tracker filter: groups of conditions with AND, OR and NOT, for Linear and GitHub** (#198). `tracker.filter` is a list of groups: every condition in a group must match (AND), an issue is read when any group matches (OR). Conditions: `projects`, `teams`, `assignee`, `labels_any`, `labels_all`, `labels_none`, `priority`, `states` (narrows `active_states`; the working state always stays in), `cycle` (`current` or an id) and `milestone`. The #182 keys (`project_slug` on Linear, `assignee`, `team`, `labels`) keep working as one implicit group; setting them and `filter` is a config error naming the keys, and an unknown condition, an empty group or a bad priority fails the load or validation. Linear compiles the filter to one `IssueFilter` (`labels.some` for any-of, one `labels.some` per label for all-of, `every` label outside the set or no labels for none-of); GitHub runs one issue search per group (`label:` / `-label:` / `assignee:` / `milestone:`, one search per label for several `labels_any`, since search has no OR between labels), unions and de-duplicates the results and keeps deriving states from the state labels; `projects`, `teams`, `priority` and `cycle` are a config error on GitHub. Every read uses the same filter — the poll, the tracker store's full and incremental pulls, webhook refreshes (checked with one shared in-memory matcher, `internal/issuefilter`), the dependency analyzer and the automation poll, whose scope key covers the whole filter so a change rebaselines without firing triggers. `domain.Issue` now carries project, team, assignees, cycle and milestone, filled by both adapters. An issue that leaves the filter mid-run finishes and is not re-dispatched; a retry waiting when its issue left the filter is now released too (its by-ID read is checked against the filter). Settings → Tracker Scope is a group builder (add/remove groups, condition pickers from the new `GET /api/v1/tracker/teams` and the existing project, label and user lists, AND/OR marked, a live debounced match count from the read-only `POST /api/v1/tracker/filter/preview`); saving goes through `PUT /api/v1/tracker/scope` with `filter`, writes `tracker.filter` as one line, comments the legacy keys out and is reload-fenced. The header chip shows one chip per group joined by OR. `itervox doctor` validates the filter, resolves its assignees (exit 1 if one is unknown) and prints how many issues it matches. Automation `filter:` accepts the same group syntax (`filter: [ ... ]` or `groups:` beside the other keys), kept through the dashboard editor. Documented in the [configuration reference](site/src/content/docs/configuration.mdx#tracker-filter), [getting started](site/src/content/docs/getting-started.mdx), the [Linear](site/src/content/docs/guides/linear-setup.mdx#filter-groups-and-or-and-not) and [GitHub](site/src/content/docs/guides/github-issues.mdx#filter-which-issues-are-read) guides, [automations](site/src/content/docs/guides/automations.mdx#groups) and [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#tracker-filter-198-linear-and-github).

- **Evals: live mode, absence checks and re-recording** (#189). The merge-bot and reviewer evals can now run against a real agent CLI: `ITERVOX_EVALS_LIVE=1 make evals-live` runs each scenario's `input.yaml` with the profile's current SOUL.md / INSTRUCTIONS.md and resolved rules, composed by the daemon's own prompt assembly (the worker's profile section moved into a shared helper, `orchestrator.ComposeEvalPrompt` reuses it), records the transcript in the `recording.jsonl` format and judges it with the existing judges. The agent runs in a throwaway sandbox where `gh` and `itervox` are shims that answer from the scenario and record every action and comment; tracker tokens are blanked. Every run is bounded by a turn cap (`claude --max-turns`), a per-scenario token cap and wall-clock timeout, and a suite cost cap, and nothing starts without `ITERVOX_EVALS_LIVE=1`, so `make verify` never spends tokens. `expected.yaml` gains `forbidden_phrases`, absence checks against every comment: the reviewer's reject path must never carry `/ai-approved` or "AI review passed", merge-bot refusals must never say "merge-bot: merged", and both profiles forbid `gh pr merge`. `make evals-record` writes `recording.candidate.jsonl` next to each fixture (never the fixture itself, and never for a failed run) and `make evals-promote SCENARIO=<profile>/<scenario>|all` replaces `recording.jsonl` after review, refusing a candidate that fails its judges unless `FORCE=1`. A new `Evals (live)` workflow runs the suite on demand (never on push or pull request) with the budget as inputs, the API key from a repository secret, and uploads transcripts and candidates as an artifact. The committed recordings are still hand-authored until the maintainer records them live. Documented in [docs/evals.md](docs/evals.md).

- **Run history records which prompt version produced each run, and what operators told it** (#186). At dispatch the daemon now computes a prompt digest — SHA-256 over a versioned, length-prefixed concatenation of the profile's `SOUL.md`, its `INSTRUCTIONS.md`, the resolved rule set (#157, sorted by id) and the prompt template (`agent.reviewer_prompt` for a reviewer that has one) — and stores it, with per-component 16-hex digests and the run ID (#125), on the run's history entry. Only hashes are kept, never prompt text, so history stays small and a secret in a profile does not spread into it. Each operator message delivered to the run from the Sessions panel (#178) — live into the running turn or as the prompt of a resumed turn — is appended to the same entry with its time and delivery path, redacted like the rest of run data, cut to 1 KiB, newest 20 kept (`steersDropped` counts the rest); typing into tmux panes is not run history. All of it is event-loop state written by `recordHistory`, persisted in the history file with backward-compatible JSON (old files load; empty fields are omitted), and survives a stall (the stall exit now also carries the run's rules hash). History rows in `/api/v1/state` gain `runId`, `profileName`, `promptDigest`, `promptParts`, `steers` and `steersDropped`; the new `GET /api/v1/history?prompt=<digest prefix>` filters the history to one prompt version and `GET /api/v1/history/prompt-versions` groups it with run counts, per-status counts, success rate and profiles per version. The dashboard's Timeline gets a **prompt version** filter listing each version with its runs and success rate, and a finished run's detail shows its short digest (copyable, part digests on hover) and its steering timeline. API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#run-history).

- **Linear tracker scope: project, assignee and labels, combined** (#182). A Linear tracker now reads the AND of three optional filters: `project_slug` (unchanged; omitted reads every project, as before), `tracker.assignee` (`me` — the API key's own user, resolved through Linear's `viewer` — a user id, or an email; optional `tracker.team` narrows it to one team) and `tracker.labels` (an issue must carry any of them). Only `assignee` reads that user's issues across every project and team the key can read; `project_slug` + `assignee` is the intersection; no existing configuration changes meaning. A dedicated "Itervox" Linear user can own the agent lane: assign a ticket to it to hand it over, reassign it to take it back. The assignee is resolved once at startup and on each `WORKFLOW.md` reload, off the event loop, and cached; one that does not resolve fails the reads (they never widen). Every read path uses the same scope: the candidate poll, `FetchIssuesByStates` (the tracker store's views, the dependency analyzer's issue set, automation polls), the store's incremental pull and the webhook refresh's by-ID scope check. An issue that leaves the scope mid-run (reassigned, its label removed, moved to another project) keeps its running worker, gets no new run or retry (a new `OutOfScope` event-loop marker; this also stops a retry from re-dispatching an issue moved out of the project filter, which the unscoped by-ID retry read used to allow), and shows "out of scope" in the dashboard and TUI. Itervox's own writes never set an assignee. The dashboard's Settings card becomes **Tracker Scope** with three independent controls — projects, assignee (anyone, me, or a workspace user; resolved before saving) and labels — saved through the new `GET`/`PUT /api/v1/tracker/scope` (with `GET /api/v1/tracker/labels` and `/tracker/users`) to `project_slug`, `assignee` and `labels` in `WORKFLOW.md` without a reload; the TUI picker (`p`) gains an "Assigned to …" toggle that combines with the projects; the header shows the combination (e.g. `ENG · assigned to me · label: agent`). The automation poll's scope key and the tracker store's scope include the assignee, team and labels, so a scope change rebaselines instead of firing triggers. A multi-project `project_slug: a, b` written by the picker is now read back as two projects after a reload. `itervox doctor` checks that the assignee resolves to a user the key can see and that the key can read its issues across its teams (exit 1 for an unresolvable assignee or an unknown team). `tracker.sync` accepts `assignee` and `labels` with its required `project_slug`. Documented in [getting started](site/src/content/docs/getting-started.mdx), the [Linear setup guide](site/src/content/docs/guides/linear-setup.mdx#scope-project-assignee-labels), the [configuration reference](site/src/content/docs/configuration.mdx) and [docs/api.md](docs/api.md).

- **Two-way sync between local issue files and Linear or GitHub** (#118). With `tracker.kind: local`, a new `tracker.sync` block (`kind: linear` or `github`, and the same `api_key`, `project_slug`, `endpoint` and state-list keys those trackers use) keeps `.itervox/issues/` in step with a Linear project or GitHub repository. A new issue file is created on the remote and gets `remote: ENG-42` / `remote: "#42"` in its front matter; a remote issue in `pull_states` becomes a new file. Title, description, state (through `state_map`), labels, priority and blockers sync both ways, and comments are copied once each way. When both sides changed a field since the last sync, the more recent edit wins on both and a comment in the file records the conflict. Per-field last-synced hashes and times live in `.itervox/sync_ledger.json` (runtime state, gitignored; a file with a `remote:` key is re-linked if it is lost), so the sync can tell which side changed and its own writes never come back as edits. Writes to the remote go through the sync's own write-ahead outbox (`.itervox/sync_outbox.json`) with coalesced push; Linear creates are idempotent under a client-generated id. Files that do not parse are skipped. The sync runs off the event loop every `tracker.sync.interval_ms` (default 60 s) and seconds after a file is saved, and the sync status (#117) shows it as mode `local_sync`. Itervox now edits an issue file's front matter in place, so YAML comments, key order and untouched values survive every rewrite. The Linear and GitHub adapters gained issue creation in their configured scope and field edits (title, description, labels, priority, blockers); on GitHub, blockers are a managed `Blocked by #3, #4` body line and state and `pN` labels are kept. Documented in the [local issues guide](site/src/content/docs/guides/local-issues.mdx).

- **Sync status: pull lag and pending writes in the dashboard, the API and doctor** (#117). `GET /api/v1/state` (and the SSE snapshot) has a new `syncStatus` object: the mode (`store` with the local tracker store, `direct` without), the last successful pull (the store's, or the last candidate poll), the lag and its warning threshold (three pull intervals, at least five minutes; `stale` past it), the store's cursor, the failed-pull run with the last sync error, and the queued tracker writes (pending, urgent, batched, retrying, degraded, rate limited, oldest, next push due, push interval). The error is classified (`rate_limited`, `auth`, `not_found`, `api_status`, `graphql`, `timeout`, `network`, `canceled`, `unknown`) with a fixed summary, never the tracker's response. The dashboard's LiveOps strip shows a sync chip ("Synced 42s ago · 3 to push"; "Sync lag 12m · last pull 10:30" in warning tone past the threshold, danger while pulls also fail; details on hover), with the lag recomputed on the dashboard's clock between pushes. `HEARTBEAT.md` has a `## Sync` section, rewritten whenever the sync status changes, and `itervox doctor` prints it and warns when the lag is past the threshold (a warning; the exit code is unchanged). Documented in [docs/api.md](docs/api.md) and [configuration](docs/configuration.md#tracker-sync-status-in-itervox-doctor).

- **Coalesced push: batched tracker writes, urgent writes first** (#115). Outbox writes now wait in a per-issue batch for `tracker.push_interval_ms` (default 10 s; `0` restores immediate pushes) before they are sent. Of the state moves queued for one issue inside a batch only the last is sent — three moves cost one tracker write and the tracker never shows the intermediate states (on GitHub this also merges the state-label swaps; Itervox writes no other labels) — and comments are posted in order. A batch's deadline is its first write's. Urgent writes skip the batch and wake the flusher at once, taking the issue's earlier queued writes with them: input-required questions and replies, the max-retries-exhausted comment, the move to `failed_state`, the rate-limit auto-switch budget-exhausted comment and operator comments from the dashboard. A queued state move shows in the local tracker store at once (board, tick, automations) while the store's own copy stays the tracker's, so reconciliation still compares against the real tracker state and never drops a queued move as already applied; the dashboard's syncing badge now covers every issue with a queued move, including one the move took out of the active states. Batched writes are durable in `.itervox/outbox.json`, so a crash before the push loses nothing: the restarted daemon pushes them when due. Only writes never handed to the flusher are merged; one already attempted keeps its retry and backoff. A flusher tick now pushes an issue's whole due batch in order instead of one write per tick.
- **Sessions panel: control sessions running in tmux, and New session** (#178). The Sessions panel can now show the screen of, and type into, an agent CLI running in a tmux pane. A Claude Code or Codex session you start by hand in tmux is matched to its pane on every 15 s discovery pass — the CLI process liveness found must be the pane's process or a descendant of it, and the pane's directory must be the session's — and gets a **tmux** badge; with the new `sessions.tmux_control: true` (off by default, read at startup) it becomes controllable: its tab shows the pane's text (`capture-pane`, polled every second while visible), a box that pastes text through a single-use tmux buffer and presses Enter (or not), and keys (Esc, Enter, ↑, ↓, 1, 2, 3, Ctrl-C with a confirmation; the daemon accepts only Enter, Escape, arrows, Tab, C-c and 1–9). **New session** starts the interactive CLI (no `-p`) in a new tmux session `itervox-<id>` in the project folder or an itervox workspace, with an optional profile and first prompt, the confining permission mode by default (`--permission-mode acceptEdits` / `--sandbox workspace-write`); itervox owns it (controllable regardless of `tmux_control`, attach command with a copy button, **Stop session** runs `tmux kill-session`), outside `max_concurrent_agents`, at most 8, carried across `WORKFLOW.md` reloads (after a restart it is a hand-started session in tmux). Before every write the pane is re-resolved (`409 pane_gone` when it is gone or no longer runs the session); every write is logged as `sessions: tmux send` with session, pane, kind and size — never the text — and counted in `itervox_tmux_sends_total{kind}`. Without tmux on the daemon's `PATH` the panel stays read-only: a banner and the composer say **tmux not found — install it to control sessions from here** with the install command (`brew install tmux` / `sudo apt install tmux`) and a copy button, New session is disabled, and every write answers `409 tmux_unavailable`; tmux is re-detected each pass, so installing it lifts the warning without a restart. New API: `GET /api/v1/sessions` gains top-level `tmux` and `newSession` and per-row `tmuxPane`, `controllable` and `attachCommand`; `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/message` takes `{text, submit}` for tmux sessions; new `GET /api/v1/sessions/{id}/screen`, `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/keys`, `POST /api/v1/sessions` and `DELETE /api/v1/sessions/{id}`. The Mac app's Sessions window shows the tmux badge and whether a session is controllable, a **New session…** entry per daemon (opens `/sessions?new=1`), and the tmux warning for a daemon without it. tmux is driven only by the new `internal/tmuxctl` (stdlib, explicit arguments); `TestNoWritesToProcessesItervoxDidNotStart` now permits writes to processes itervox did not start only there, and fails if any other package runs `tmux` or names its write commands or if `tmuxctl` runs anything else. **Anyone holding the dashboard token can type into opted-in tmux sessions.** Guides: [Sessions panel → Sessions in tmux](site/src/content/docs/guides/sessions.mdx#sessions-in-tmux), [Mac app → Sessions window](site/src/content/docs/guides/mac-app.mdx#sessions-window); API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#sessions-in-tmux); config: [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md#sessions).
- **Sessions panel: sessions started by hand, read-only** (#178, step 3). The Sessions panel now also lists the Claude Code and Codex sessions started by hand on the daemon's host — discovered off the event loop every 15 s from `~/.claude/projects/<encoded-dir>/<id>.jsonl` and `~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-*.jsonl` (both Codex layouts; `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` / `$CODEX_HOME` respected), with tolerant parsers that skip records they do not know — as `owner: "external"` tabs after itervox's own, greyed and labelled **started outside itervox**. By default only sessions written to in the last 24 hours whose working directory is inside the project (the `WORKFLOW.md` directory) are listed, never itervox's own sessions or anything under its workspace root; the new `sessions:` block sets `external`, `external_window_hours`, `external_scope` (`project` / `all`) and `external_roots`. A tab shows the CLI's own transcript (new `GET /api/v1/sessions/{id}/transcript`, paged backwards, redacted with the log redaction, tool calls by name, thinking and sidechains left out). Each tab says **running** while the original CLI may still be running and **exited** once it is not — decided read-only (`/proc` on Linux, `ps` and `lsof` on macOS, no privacy permission) and conservatively: its transcript open, its session ID in a process's arguments, a `claude`/`codex` process in its directory, an unreadable process list, or a write in the last two minutes all count as running, with the reason shown. Such sessions stay read-only either way: messages to them are refused with `403 not_owned`. The Mac app's Sessions window lists hand-started sessions after each daemon's own (dashed, **started outside itervox**, **running** with the reason on hover, or **exited**). A new static test, `TestExternalSessionInspectionIsReadOnly`, keeps the discovery and liveness code free of writes, signals and any command but `ps` and `lsof`; `TestNoWritesToProcessesItervoxDidNotStart` still passes. Guides: [Sessions panel → Sessions started by hand](site/src/content/docs/guides/sessions.mdx#sessions-started-by-hand), [Mac app → Sessions window](site/src/content/docs/guides/mac-app.mdx#sessions-window); API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#sessions); config: [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md#sessions).

- **Sessions panel: tabs over running agent sessions, with a composer** (#178, steps 1–2). A new dashboard page, **Sessions** (`/sessions`), has one tab per agent session of the daemon — every running itervox run and every session waiting for input — identified by the agent CLI's own session ID (the run ID until the CLI reports one). Sessions waiting for input are badged and listed first (the sidebar icon counts them); arrow keys, Home and End move between tabs, and `?id=` selects one. Each tab shows the issue's live log and a composer: for a session waiting for input, the existing reply box (`provide-input`, which resumes the same session); for a running session, an operator message sent with the new `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/message`, shown as queued, delivered live, delivered on resume, or not delivered with the reason. A message reaches a local Claude worker mid-turn when the new `agent.live_steering: true` is set (the turn runs with `--input-format stream-json`, the prompt is the first stdin message, the operator's is written as a further user message, and stdin closes at the turn's result); otherwise — and always for Codex (`exec` takes no input while it runs) and SSH workers — it is queued and delivered as the prompt of a turn that resumes the same session (`--resume` / `exec resume`) as soon as the current turn ends. `GET /api/v1/sessions` lists the sessions with id, run, owner, issue, profile, backend, host, status (`running` / `input_required` / `pending_input_resume`), start time and messages. Progress updates now carry the CLI's session ID from the first stream event, so a first turn is addressable before it ends. The Mac app has a **Sessions…** menu item (with the number waiting) that opens a Sessions window listing the sessions of every daemon — local and remote through their tunnels — grouped by daemon, waiting ones first; choosing one opens that daemon's dashboard at `/sessions?id=…` with the usual token handoff. Itervox writes only to agent processes it started: no TTY injection and no Accessibility or AppleScript automation, enforced by the static test `TestNoWritesToProcessesItervoxDidNotStart`. Messages are runtime state (not persisted). Guides: [Sessions panel](site/src/content/docs/guides/sessions.mdx), [Mac app → Sessions window](site/src/content/docs/guides/mac-app.mdx#sessions-window); API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#sessions).

- **Mac app: remote daemons over IAP and SSH tunnels** (#156). **Add Remote…** in the menu-bar app reaches daemons on a cloud VM or another machine: over SSH (`user@host` or a `~/.ssh/config` alias) or GCP IAP (SSH through IAP, as the deployment kit sets up, or a direct `gcloud compute start-iap-tunnel` to the daemon port). The app runs `itervox status --all --json` on the host over the same transport, lists every daemon there, and gives each chosen daemon its own tunnel on its own free local port (`ssh -N -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -o ServerAliveInterval=15 -L 127.0.0.1:<local>:127.0.0.1:<port>`, or the `gcloud` equivalent); two daemons never share a port, also while one is reconnecting, and a daemon keeps its port across reconnects and app restarts when it is free. Every 2 seconds each tunnel is checked (process alive, TCP connect, `GET /api/v1/health` through it); a tunnel whose process exits, or that fails three checks in a row, is restarted with backoff (1 s doubling to 30 s), and after the Mac wakes from sleep or its network changes every tunnel is re-probed at once and a dead one restarted at once — no user action. Remote daemons' tokens are read from the daemon's `token_file` over the transport, or typed in, and stored in the login Keychain (`dev.itervox.desktop.remote-token`) under the remote and the daemon's remote `WORKFLOW.md` path, never the local port, so two remotes never share a token; agent credentials stay on the host. Opening a remote dashboard uses the tunnel URL with the same token handoff as a local one, and questions and failed runs on remote daemons notify too. The menu has a **Remotes** section with each connection's state (`2/2 connected`, `reconnecting…`) and per daemon **Open Dashboard** and **Enter/Update Token…**, plus **Reconnect**, **Refresh Daemon List** and **Remove Remote**. Remotes are kept in `remotes.json` in the app's config directory; `ssh` and `gcloud` are found through the login shell's `PATH`, so an app started from Finder finds them. Guide: [Mac app → Remote daemons](site/src/content/docs/guides/mac-app.mdx#remote-daemons).
- **Mac app: signed, notarized releases that update themselves** (#130). Each release tag now also publishes a universal `Itervox_<version>_universal.dmg` and a universal `itervox_<version>_darwin_universal.zip` CLI, built by the new `Desktop release` workflow (called from `Release` after GoReleaser): the CLI and the app — with the bundled daemon signed inside it — are signed with a Developer ID certificate imported into a temporary keychain, with the hardened runtime and `desktop/src-tauri/Entitlements.plist` (network client and server only), notarized with `notarytool` (an App Store Connect API key, or an Apple ID with an app-specific password), stapled, and the job fails unless `codesign --verify --deep --strict` and `spctl --assess --type execute` accept the app as `Notarized Developer ID`; the disk image is signed, notarized and checked too. Without the Apple secrets (forks) it builds `-unsigned` files with a warning, and it refuses a half-configured secret set. The app now updates itself with `tauri-plugin-updater`: it reads `latest.json` from the latest GitHub release 10 seconds after launch, every 6 hours and on **Check for Updates…**, shows **Update available — Install and Restart**, verifies the archive against the updater public key in `tauri.conf.json` (a build without one shows **Updates off**), replaces itself in place and relaunches; the workflow writes `latest.json` and the signed `.app.tar.gz` (uploading the manifest last). The bundled daemon updates with the app, and the new **Install Command-Line Tool…** menu item links `itervox` in `/usr/local/bin` (or `~/.local/bin`) to it, so that command follows every update; an `itervox` the app did not install is never replaced. Running daemons are detached and keep running through an update on their old version until restarted. Setup, secrets, the updater key and local verification commands: [docs/release-mac.md](docs/release-mac.md); guide: [Mac app](site/src/content/docs/guides/mac-app.mdx).

- **Mac app: a menu-bar shell over the daemons** (#128). A Tauri v2 app in `desktop/` with the daemon bundled as its sidecar and the existing dashboard reused as is. From the menu bar it lists every daemon `itervox status --all --json` reports plus the projects you add (kept in the app's `projects.json`), each with its state, running agents and questions waiting, refreshed every 3 seconds; starts a project's daemon headless and detached (so it survives quitting the app) with a freshly generated `ITERVOX_SUPERVISOR_TOKEN` stored in the login Keychain, stops it with `SIGTERM` to its registered pid, and restarts it, each reflected at the next refresh; raises a macOS notification when an issue starts waiting for input or a run fails, and clicking it opens that issue in the dashboard (`?issue=`); and opens a project's dashboard in a window, handing it the token through an origin-checked initialization script instead of a URL. It runs the daemon bundled next to its own executable, never one found on PATH, and the daemon resolves PATH from the login shell (#119), so no terminal is needed. Daemons started from a terminal show their state too when their token is auto-generated (read from `token_file`), else "token required". `make desktop` builds the unsigned app (`make desktop-sidecar` builds the daemon for both Mac architectures), `make desktop-test` runs fmt, clippy, the unit tests and end-to-end tests against a real daemon, and the new `Desktop CI` workflow runs both on a macOS runner and uploads the unsigned bundle; signing and notarization are #130. Guide: [Mac app](site/src/content/docs/guides/mac-app.mdx).

- **Mac-app groundwork: `itervox status --json`, supervisor token, login-shell PATH** (#119). `itervox status --all --json` prints a JSON array with one object per running daemon on the host — `pid`, `workflow`, `project_dir`, `url`, `host`, `port`, `version`, `commit`, `started_at`, `token_required`, `token_source`, `token_file`, `logs_dir`, `heartbeat`, `executable`, `path_source`, `source` — and `status --json` the same for this project only; the format is versioned (`schema_version: 1`) and documented as the supervisor contract in [docs/api.md](docs/api.md#supervisor-contract). It reads a new host registry: each daemon writes `~/.itervox/daemons/<pid>.json` (`0600`, in a `0700` directory; never a token) when its port is bound, rewrites it on reload and removes it on shutdown; a record whose daemon died is skipped and deleted — including when its pid was recycled by another process, since the daemon's pid lock must still be held — all published paths are absolute (a relative `--logs-dir` is resolved against the daemon's working directory), and daemons started by older binaries are still found by process scan. `itervox demo` writes no record. `ITERVOX_SUPERVISOR_TOKEN` is the token a supervisor (the coming macOS app) starts the daemon with: the API requires it — over a different `ITERVOX_API_TOKEN` and over `server.allow_unauthenticated: true` — and it is never printed or written: no tokenised dashboard URL on stderr even on a terminal or with `ITERVOX_PRINT_TOKEN=1`, none in the terminal UI, the log file, `HEARTBEAT.md`, `dashboard_url`, the registry or `api-token`; a malformed value (under 16 or over 512 characters, spaces, non-ASCII) stops the process with exit code 2. When the daemon was not started from an interactive shell (Finder, launchd, systemd), or an agent CLI the workflow names is missing from its PATH, it now takes PATH from the user's login shell (`$SHELL -l -i -c` — for csh/tcsh `$SHELL -c` after sourcing `/etc/csh.login` and `~/.login` — once at startup, bounded to 5 seconds, no terminal, the PATH taken byte for byte), so `claude` and `codex` installed through nvm, asdf or Homebrew are found; `ITERVOX_LOGIN_SHELL_PATH=always|never` overrides the decision. The startup log says where PATH came from, `itervox doctor` prints a `PATH source:` line and where each agent CLI resolves (a missing one is a warning), and `status --json` reports `path_source`. Documented in the [CLI reference](site/src/content/docs/cli.mdx#itervox-status--list-running-daemons).
- **Settings page from the config schema; `itervox import` and `itervox export --symphony`** (#158).
